questions.stem: Which of these is NOT one of the organization's vulnerabilities?

options.rationale: Correct choice: that is a threat, not a weakness.

options.text: A software flaw in a web application
A weak process for approving firewall changes

questions.explanation: Vulnerabilities are weaknesses that can be exploited: software flaws, misconfigurations, and weak processes. A ransomware gang is a threat.
questions.discriminator_tested: A vulnerability is the weakness itself.

questions.stem: Which two activities are part of vulnerability identification? (Choose two.)

options.text: Checking threat intelligence for flaws that affect your inventory

questions.explanation: Vulnerability identification discovers weaknesses through scans, testing, inventories, and threat intelligence. You can't fix what you haven't found.
questions.discriminator_tested: Identification uses scans, testing, inventories, and threat intelligence.

questions.stem: Which statement about vulnerability management is NOT true?

options.text: A single annual scan completes it
options.rationale: Correct choice because it is false: it is a continuous cycle.

options.text: It includes verifying that fixes worked

questions.explanation: Vulnerability management is an ongoing cycle: identify, prioritize, remediate or mitigate, verify, and report. It is a continuous process, not a one-time scan.
questions.discriminator_tested: Continuous process, not a one-time scan.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT an example of vulnerability mitigation?

options.text: Installing the vendor patch that removes the flaw
options.rationale: Correct choice: removing the flaw is remediation.

options.text: Moving the system to an isolated network segment
Adding an ACL that limits who can reach the system
Disabling the vulnerable service until a fix arrives

questions.explanation: Vulnerability mitigation reduces exposure when a full fix isn't immediately possible, through segmentation, ACLs, or disabling the service. Patching is remediation, which removes the flaw.
questions.discriminator_tested: Mitigation lowers risk; remediation removes the flaw.

questions.stem: In active vs passive reconnaissance, why is passive reconnaissance harder for the target to notice?

options.text: Passive reconnaissance doesn't touch the target, so nothing reaches its logs; active reconnaissance interacts directly and can be logged

options.rationale: Passive reconnaissance sends no traffic to the target at all.

options.text: They are equally easy to notice
options.rationale: Only active reconnaissance touches the target.

questions.explanation: Active vs passive reconnaissance: passive gathers information without touching the target; active interacts with it directly. Active can be detected and logged; passive generally can't.
questions.discriminator_tested: Active can be detected and logged; passive generally can't.

questions.stem:
A port scan of a public web server reports:

22/tcp   open  ssh
443/tcp  open  https
3306/tcp open  mysql

What can you conclude, and what can't you conclude?

options.text: These services are listening and reachable (an exposed database port is a concern), but the scan doesn't show whether they have known vulnerabilities
options.rationale: Correct: open ports aren't the same as known flaws.

options.text: The scan proves all three services are vulnerable
options.rationale: A port scan doesn't check for flaws.

options.text: The scan lists the CVEs for each service
options.rationale: Listing CVEs is a vulnerability scan's job.

questions.explanation: Port scanning probes hosts for open ports and running services. It is active and finds open ports only, not known flaws; checking for known flaws takes a vulnerability scan.
questions.discriminator_tested: A port scan finds open ports, not known flaws.

questions.stem: Which statement about vulnerability scanning is NOT true?

options.text: It only lists open ports, exactly like a port scan
options.rationale: Correct choice because it is false: it checks services against known vulnerabilities.

options.text: It checks systems against known vulnerabilities
It can be credentialed or non-credentialed
It goes beyond what a port scan reports

questions.explanation: Vulnerability scanning runs automated checks of systems against known vulnerabilities, either credentialed or non-credentialed. It reports known weaknesses, going beyond a port scan.
questions.discriminator_tested: Vulnerability scanning reports known weaknesses.

questions.stem: An analyst wants to find out which protocols on a network segment still send credentials in cleartext. Which technique fits?

options.rationale: Correct: it shows what actually crosses the network.
A port scan shows open ports, not credentials in traffic.
Brute force guesses passwords; it doesn't observe traffic.

questions.explanation: Packet sniffing, or network traffic analysis, captures and examines traffic to show protocols, cleartext credentials, and anomalies.
questions.discriminator_tested: Sniffing reveals what crosses the network.

questions.stem: Which statement about brute-force attacks used in testing is NOT true?

options.text: They are passive and leave no trace in the target's logs
options.rationale: Correct choice because it is false: they are active and noisy.

questions.explanation: Brute-force attacks try many credential combinations to test or break password strength. They are active and noisy, and lockouts counter them.
questions.discriminator_tested: Brute force is active and noisy.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT an OSINT activity?

options.text: Running a vulnerability scan against the company's servers
options.rationale: Correct choice: that touches the target, so it is active.

questions.explanation: OSINT is information gathered from public sources such as websites, social media, public records, and job posts. It is passive, with no direct contact with the target.
questions.discriminator_tested: OSINT is passive, from public sources.

questions.stem: A tester wants to map all of a company's subdomains and DNS records. Which technique fits?

options.rationale: Correct: it maps the domain's DNS footprint.

options.text: Packet sniffing on the tester's own laptop
options.rationale: That shows local traffic, not the company's DNS records.

questions.explanation: DNS enumeration discovers a domain's hostnames, subdomains, and records. It is passive from public records and active when it queries the target's DNS servers.
questions.discriminator_tested: DNS enumeration maps the DNS footprint.

questions.stem: Which statement about social engineering as a reconnaissance technique is NOT true?

options.text: It is passive, because no computer is touched
options.rationale: Correct choice because it is false: it is active, because it interacts with the target's people.

options.text: It manipulates people into revealing information
It can be done by phone or in person

questions.explanation: Social engineering as reconnaissance means manipulating people to reveal information. It is human-based and active.
questions.discriminator_tested: Social engineering reconnaissance is active.

questions.stem: Which statement about testing in a vulnerability assessment is NOT true?

options.text: It can be done without authorization, as long as it is quiet
options.rationale: Correct choice because it is false: testing must be authorized.

options.text: It confirms what scans only suggest

questions.explanation: Testing is a set of systematic, authorized checks to find and confirm weaknesses. It is authorized and scoped, and it confirms what scans suggest.
questions.discriminator_tested: Testing is authorized and scoped.

questions.stem: Which two are benefits of automation in vulnerability assessment? (Choose two.)

options.text: Consistent results from run to run
No need for any human review
options.rationale: The results still need review and prioritization.
Automated tools do produce false positives.
Scanning finds problems; it doesn't fix them.

questions.explanation: Automation means scheduled, scripted, tool-driven scans and checks: fast, consistent, and repeatable at scale. The results still need human review and prioritization.
questions.discriminator_tested: Automation is fast and consistent, but still needs human review.

questions.stem: A team wants to know which attacker groups target its industry and which indicators of their activity to watch for. What does it need?

options.rationale: Correct: external context about actors, tactics, and indicators.
That finds weaknesses in your own systems.

questions.explanation: Threat intelligence is information about threats, actors, tactics, and indicators, used to anticipate and defend. It is external, actionable context.
questions.discriminator_tested: Threat intelligence is external, actionable context.

questions.stem: Which pairing related to vulnerability databases is NOT correct?

options.text: CVSS: the unique identifier for each vulnerability
options.rationale: Correct choice because it is wrong: the identifier is the CVE; CVSS is the severity score.

questions.explanation: Vulnerability databases are public catalogs of known vulnerabilities. CVE is the identifier, the NVD is the enriched database, and CVSS is the severity score.
questions.discriminator_tested: CVE = identifier; NVD = database; CVSS = score.

questions.stem: Which two are limitations of vulnerability databases? (Choose two.)

options.text: Their scores don't reflect your own environment
options.rationale: Correct: a high score may matter little where you are.

options.text: They list every flaw before it is ever exploited

options.rationale: Databases list flaws; they don't fix them.
You still need to find which flaws affect your systems.

questions.explanation: Limitations of vulnerability databases: they lag behind new discoveries, their data can be incomplete or inconsistent, and their scores lack your environment's context. They don't list zero-day flaws.
questions.discriminator_tested: No zero-days; scores lack your environment's context.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT an assessment tool?

options.text: An RSS reader for security news
options.rationale: Correct choice: it delivers news; it doesn't assess systems.

questions.explanation: Assessment tools assess systems: vulnerability scanners, port scanners, and configuration auditors. They automate discovery, and their output still needs analysis.
questions.discriminator_tested: Assessment tools assess systems.

questions.stem: What makes recommendations in an assessment report useful?

options.text: They are specific, prioritized, and actionable guidance tied to the findings
They are vague, so they apply to everyone
options.rationale: Vague advice can't be acted on.

options.text: They are unranked, so all look equally important
options.rationale: Without priority, teams don't know where to start.

questions.explanation: Recommendations are the specific, prioritized guidance that comes out of an assessment. They are its actionable output.
questions.discriminator_tested: Recommendations are specific, prioritized, and actionable.

questions.stem: Which action does NOT reduce the surface area for attack?

options.rationale: Correct choice: more software means more exposure.

questions.explanation: To reduce the surface area for attack, disable unneeded services, ports, accounts, and software. Fewer exposed components means fewer vulnerabilities.
questions.discriminator_tested: Fewer components means fewer vulnerabilities.

questions.stem: Which statement about Group Policy is NOT true?

options.text: It manages settings on Linux servers through SELinux
options.rationale: Correct choice because it is false: Group Policy manages Windows; SELinux is a separate Linux mechanism.

options.text: It centrally manages settings on Windows computers
It applies to both users and computers

questions.explanation: Group Policy centrally manages and enforces settings on Windows computers and users. It provides central enforcement of configuration and security settings.
questions.discriminator_tested: Group Policy centrally enforces Windows settings.

questions.stem: In which order are GPOs applied, when none are enforced or blocked?

options.rationale: Correct: later ones override earlier ones.
Local comes first, and OU comes last.

questions.explanation: GPOs are bundles of settings linked to a site, domain, or OU. They apply in the order local, site, domain, then OU, and later ones override earlier ones.
questions.discriminator_tested: Local, site, domain, OU; later overrides earlier.

questions.stem: Which statement about local group policy is NOT true?

options.text: It applies to every computer in the domain
options.rationale: Correct choice because it is false: its scope is one machine.

options.text: Its scope is a single machine
It works on computers that aren't in a domain
Domain policy overrides it on conflict

questions.explanation: Local group policy is the set of settings applied to a single computer, so its scope is one machine. Domain group policy covers many machines and overrides local on conflict.
questions.discriminator_tested: Local group policy's scope is one machine.

questions.stem: An administrator changes a setting in the local policy of a domain-joined PC, but after the next policy refresh it reverts. Why?

options.text: A domain GPO sets it differently, and domain group policy overrides local policy on conflict
Local policy always wins, so it must be a bug
options.rationale: Local policy is applied first and is overridden.

questions.explanation: Domain group policy applies settings centrally through Active Directory and overrides local settings on conflict. That is why the local change keeps reverting at refresh.
questions.discriminator_tested: Domain policy overrides local on conflict.

questions.stem: What is the difference between SELinux enforcing mode and permissive mode?

options.text: Enforcing blocks and logs violations; permissive only logs them
Permissive blocks violations; enforcing only logs them

options.rationale: That is disabled mode; permissive still checks and logs.

questions.explanation: SELinux mode is enforcing, permissive, or disabled (check with getenforce; switch with setenforce). Enforcing blocks and logs violations; permissive only logs them.
questions.discriminator_tested: Enforcing blocks and logs; permissive only logs.

questions.stem: Which is NOT a recommended way to reduce the attack surface of Samba?

options.rationale: Correct choice: SMBv1 should be disabled.

options.text: Disabling Samba if it isn't used

questions.explanation: Samba is the Linux/Unix implementation of SMB file and print sharing. Exposed SMB is attack surface: disable it if unused, restrict shares, require authentication, disable SMBv1, and keep it patched.
questions.discriminator_tested: Disable SMBv1; restrict, authenticate, and patch.

questions.stem: Which is NOT a good practice for security reports?

options.text: Giving the board raw scanner output with no summary
options.rationale: Correct choice: executives need an executive summary.

options.text: Tailoring the report to its audience

questions.explanation: Security reports summarize assessment findings, vulnerabilities, and recommendations. Tailor them to the audience: technical detail for IT, an executive summary for leadership.
questions.discriminator_tested: Tailor reports to the audience.

questions.stem: Which statement about cybersecurity news as an information source is NOT true?

options.text: Any headline can be acted on immediately, without verification
options.rationale: Correct choice because it is false: verify credibility first.

questions.explanation: Cybersecurity news sources report emerging threats and vulnerabilities. They build awareness, but their credibility should be verified before acting.
questions.discriminator_tested: Verify credibility before acting.

questions.stem: Which statement about subscription-based sources of threat intelligence is NOT true?

options.rationale: Correct choice because it is false: they are paid or subscribed.

options.text: They are often deeper than free sources

questions.explanation: Subscription-based sources are paid or subscribed threat-intelligence feeds and advisories. They are curated, timely, and often deeper than free sources, but they cost money.
questions.discriminator_tested: Subscription sources are curated and timely, but cost money.

questions.stem: Which statement about an RSS feed is NOT true?

options.text: You have to visit each site by hand to see its new items
options.rationale: Correct choice because it is false: the feed brings new items to you.

options.text: It comes from sites you choose

questions.explanation: An RSS feed delivers new items from chosen sites automatically, pulling updates to you without visiting each site.
questions.discriminator_tested: RSS pulls updates to you.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a benefit of documentation?

options.text: It lets changes skip review, because they are already written down
options.rationale: Correct choice: documentation doesn't replace review.

options.text: It records processes, changes, and events

questions.explanation: Documentation is the written record of processes, changes, and events. It makes actions repeatable and auditable.
questions.discriminator_tested: Documentation makes actions repeatable and auditable.

questions.stem: Which practice is NOT part of updating documentation?

options.text: Updating documents only once every five years
options.rationale: Correct choice: documents go stale between changes.

questions.explanation: Updating documentation means keeping documents current as systems, processes, and lessons change. Outdated documentation misleads responders.
questions.discriminator_tested: Keep documentation current; outdated documents mislead.

questions.stem: Which two items belong in security incident documentation? (Choose two.)

options.text: The actions taken, and who took them

questions.explanation: Security incident documentation is a record of the incident: the timeline, affected systems, actions taken, and who did what. It is a factual, time-stamped account.
questions.discriminator_tested: Factual, time-stamped account of the incident.

questions.stem:
An evidence log reads:

09:05  Drive imaged by A. Lee (hash recorded)
09:40  Drive handed from A. Lee to B. Cruz
11:15  Drive sealed in evidence locker 3 by B. Cruz

Why does this log matter?

options.text: It is a complete chain of custody (who handled the evidence, when, and how), which supports its integrity and admissibility
options.rationale: Correct: there are no unexplained gaps.

options.text: It doesn't matter; only the image itself does
options.rationale: Without the handling record, the image's integrity can be challenged.

options.text: It replaces the need for a hash
options.rationale: The log and the hash support each other.

options.text: It is needed only for insurance claims
options.rationale: It matters for any investigation or legal use.

questions.explanation: Chain of custody is the documented trail of who handled evidence, when, and how. A gap undermines the integrity and admissibility of evidence; this log has none.
questions.discriminator_tested: A complete chain of custody supports integrity and admissibility.

questions.stem: Which statement about reporting incidents is NOT true?

options.text: Regulators can be left out if management would prefer it
options.rationale: Correct choice because it is false: mandated reporting can't be skipped by preference.

options.text: Some reporting deadlines are set by regulation
Customers may need to be notified

questions.explanation: Reporting incidents means notifying the right parties (management, security team, legal, regulators, customers) according to policy. Follow the defined reporting path; some timing is mandated by regulation.
questions.discriminator_tested: Follow the defined path; mandated reporting can't be skipped.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT part of incident recovery?

options.text: Holding a meeting to decide whom to blame
options.rationale: Correct choice: blame isn't part of recovery, and the later review aims at improvement, not blame.

questions.explanation: Incident recovery restores affected systems to normal operation (clean backups, rebuild, validate). It is the return to service after containment.
questions.discriminator_tested: Recovery restores systems to normal operation.

questions.stem: When should reviewing the incident (the post-incident review) take place?

options.text: After recovery, once systems are back in normal operation

options.rationale: Reconnaissance isn't part of incident handling.

questions.explanation: Reviewing the incident is a post-incident review to find the root cause and improve controls. It happens after recovery and aims at improvement, not blame.
questions.discriminator_tested: The review happens after recovery.

questions.stem: Which practice is NOT one of the documentation best practices?

options.text: Storing incident documents in a public folder for convenience
options.rationale: Correct choice: they can contain sensitive details and must be stored securely.

questions.explanation: Documentation best practices: clear, accurate, timely, consistent, version-controlled, and securely stored. Document as you go, and protect the documents because they can contain sensitive details.
questions.discriminator_tested: Store documentation securely; it can be sensitive.
